chapter_theme: Songs at Viruthachalam (விருத்தாசலம், முதுகிரி): the poet rejects courtesans who sell themselves and strip men of wealth, asks for grace among the loveless, and describes old age with staff and failing eyes as a birth to be freed from; the praise names Murugan who taught Siva and impaled the Jains.
structure_note: 750 on courtesans, 751 mostly praise with a short plea, 752 on old age.

750.reading: The poet describes women with breasts like lotus pots, moon brows, hair like cloud, carp eyes, voices like the yaazh, parrot and cuckoo, and the gait of peacocks, who mock the many lustful men, smile like lightning and strip of wealth those who kiss them, women who sell themselves, and asks whether their friendship befits him. The praise names Rama who bridged the sea and destroyed Ravana's clan as uncle, Siva who cut Brahma's head and burned the cities, Uma in Siva's half, the vel that uprooted the poisonous asuras and freed the gods, Murugan the beautiful one of the hunter girl, at Viruthachalam where 'my mother' dwells.
750.nuance: விலைமாதர், women with a price, and பொருள் பறிப்பார், who snatch wealth, make the charge explicit. என தாய் உறை விருத்தாசலம names the shrine's goddess as the poet's own mother.

751.reading: Mostly praise: Murugan, born in the pond, once gave Siva the holy word as Siva served at his side; at Madurai he sent the Jains to the stake; he came to Arunai in an instant so the whole world praised him; he became a tree before the hunter girl's eyes; he is Hari's nephew and the first one who speaks in compassion. In the middle the poet, suffering among those who have no love for Murugan's grace, asks whether he will be given grace, at Mudhukiri, the old hill.
751.nuance: அரன் உனது உழி பணி செய முன் அருளிய: Siva serves at Murugan's side to receive the word, the teaching of Om in the book's usual story, here without naming Om. அருணையில் ஒருநொடி தனில் வரு மயில்வீரா refers to an appearance at Tiruvannamalai, which tradition ties to the poet's own life; the text says only that he came in a moment. The last line (முடிபவர் வடிவறு சுசிகர முறைதமிழ்) is obscure.

752.reading: The poet describes old age: the body dried and sapless as deeds ripen, the gait tottering, the hands scratching, the teeth bare, eyes blinded by cataract, skin wrinkled like fruit, hair white as a crane, bile and wind rising, weak, gripping a staff and left standing outside; he asks whether there will be a day when Murugan frees him from this birth of suffering and sets grace on him. The praise names the gods led by Indra who covered the earth with flowers after Murugan's victory over the asuras, Krishna as his uncle, and the Siva devotees who sang sweet words and won grace at Viruddhagiri.
752.nuance: The portrait of age is built of small physical signs, and its last image, வெளிநிற்கும் விதம், standing outside the house, adds the social exclusion of the old. The plea is not against age itself but against the birth (ஜனனம்) that leads to it. The Siva devotees who won grace with sweet words may be the Tevaram poets; the text does not name them.

links.note: Both picture old age by faltering steps, the staff and fallen teeth; the Naladiyar faults the old man still clinging to desire, 752 asks to be freed from the birth that brings such an end.
Both tie the courtesan's favour to money: the Naladiyar says a rich oil-presser is sugar to her, 750 that she strips of wealth the men she kisses.
